doc.title: Neal Caine interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019

title: Elvin on Coltrane and the broken end pin
summary: Elvin loved Coltrane and spoke of Basie and Duke; he scolded Caine for stopping when the end pin broke at the New Morning; Elvin and Betty's seriousness.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: If an interviewer, you know, got an interview with him and opened the first thing they said was, “Mr. Jones tell us about John Coltrane.” How would be react to that?

Well it would probably depend on his mood at that particular moment, but he would say he was an angel. He loved John Coltrane. He was a genius and an angel. I mean he used to talk about, I mean I was lucky enough to spend some time with him and he loved — he used to talk about the Basie band, Duke’s band, and then like you know one time I remember we were playing at the New Morning. And it would be like an open bass solo. And I was doing my kind of Jimmy, you know my thing. And my end pin broke. And maybe I stopped for a second and I came off the stage afterwards. And he was mad at me. He was yelling at me, “Why’d you stop?” And I was like, “Man, the bass broke bro.” And he was like, “Wilbur Ware played a bass made out of milk cartons.” You know like it would be shit like that. I mean it was actually a little more colorful language and all that, but he was a great man. He didn’t give a fuck. That’s what I mean, the old school, same thing with Betty Carter. They weren’t having it man. It was about making sure the music was right. Like there was a certain seriousness — it’s hard to translate, and it sounds cliché but it’s true, there was a certain seriousness that like Elvin and Betty took that they had about this music, that I don’t know that many other people in our generation have. It’s actually life and death type shit.

I think I know what you’re saying, because I’ve been fortunate to interview a lot of folks from that generation, and they’re serious. And they’re always dressed up and they’re always a take care of the bandstand type attitude. Why would that change? © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
